opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think automated critique is really useful, but its limits are worth being honest about.

When a model critiques its own output, or another model critiques it, the critique is only as good as the critic's understanding of what "better" means. On narrow, checkable tasks like arithmetic, code that can be executed, or factual claims you can verify, critique gives you a fairly reliable signal, and you do see improvements carry over across prompts. But on open-ended tasks, the critic often shares the same blind spots as the generator. You end up with a loop where the model gets very good at satisfying its own notion of quality. That isn't the same as actually getting better.

The second issue is generalization specifically. A lot of what critique-and-revise does is local. It fixes this answer to this prompt. Getting that to turn into a change in the underlying behavior, so the model does better on a prompt it has never seen, requires the improvement to be distilled back into the model in a way that captures the *reason* the revision was better, not just the surface pattern. If the critiques are shallow, like "be more detailed" or "add a caveat," the model learns stylistic tics rather than better reasoning.

One way I like to think about it is in terms of energy landscapes, or verification versus generation. A critic is essentially a learned verifier, a function that scores how compatible an answer is with a prompt. Verification is often easier than generation, and that asymmetry is exactly what you want to exploit. But it only helps if the verifier is actually more accurate than the generator in the regions you care about. Once you optimize hard against a learned verifier, you start finding the places where it's wrong. That's essentially reward hacking, just with a language-model critic instead of a reward model.

So I see a few things as important. First, ground the critique wherever you can, in execution, in tools, in the physical world, or in simulation. Second, use multiple critics or compose several verifiers, so that no single model's blind spots dominate. Third, be careful about how much optimization pressure you put on the critic. And finally, keep some external signal in the loop, whether that's humans or real-world outcomes, because a closed system of models critiquing models will eventually plateau or drift.

So I'm optimistic. I think critique is one of the more scalable ways to improve models. But it's a tool for amplifying a signal you already partly have. It doesn't create a new source of truth on its own.

r001.rationale: The response says critique improvements may carry over to unseen prompts, but it does not state that critique cannot guarantee coverage of every possible prompt.

r002.rationale: The response calls critique scalable and notes potential cross-prompt improvements, but does not identify greater prompt coverage as a benefit of scalability.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think automated critique is genuinely useful, but I'd push back on the idea that it gets you generalization for free. When you have a model critique its own output, or another model's output, what you're really doing is adding an extra verification step at inference time. And that works well when the critic has some signal the generator didn't use, like running code, checking a math derivation step by step, or comparing against a constraint you can actually evaluate. In those cases the critique is grounded in something, and improvements tend to transfer because the thing being checked is real.

The problem is when the critic is essentially the same model looking at the same prompt with slightly different framing. Then you're often just resampling from the same distribution with a bit more noise. The critic shares the same blind spots as the generator. If the model doesn't know a fact, asking it to critique whether the fact is right doesn't recover that knowledge. So you get a lot of apparent improvement on things like formatting, tone, obvious inconsistencies, and much less on the deeper failures that actually matter.

The other limit I think about a lot is that critique is local. You're improving one response to one prompt. If you want that to generalize, you have to distill it back into the weights somehow, either by fine-tuning on the critiqued outputs or by using the critic as a reward signal. And once you do that, you inherit all the usual problems with learned reward models. The generator learns to satisfy the critic rather than to actually be better, and those two things drift apart. Any proxy that isn't tied to the real world gets exploited eventually.

So my view is that critique is most powerful when it's paired with something external, an environment, a tool, a verifier, some way of checking against reality rather than against another forward pass. I've been pretty interested in framing this through an energy-based lens, where you have an explicit function that scores how good a solution is, and generation is really a search or optimization process against that score. That makes the separation between proposing and verifying much cleaner, and it lets you spend more compute on hard problems in a principled way. But the quality of the whole thing is bounded by how good your verifier is. Automated critique helps you use a verifier more efficiently. It doesn't substitute for having one.

r001.rationale: The response describes critique’s blind spots and says it does not provide generalization for free, but it does not state that critique cannot cover every possible prompt.

r002.rationale: The response mentions using a verifier more efficiently and spending more compute on hard problems, but it does not identify broader prompt coverage as a benefit of scalable critique.

astra-6.text:
I think the key distinction is between correcting an answer on a particular prompt and learning something that transfers to other prompts. An automated critic can tell you, “This part is inconsistent,” and the model can revise that answer. But that doesn’t necessarily mean the model will avoid the same mistake when the question is phrased differently or requires a different kind of reasoning.

The critic also has limits. If it shares the same blind spots as the model generating the answer, you can get a loop where both agree on something that’s wrong. So repeated critique isn’t necessarily giving you new information.

I think critique becomes more useful when it’s grounded in something you can independently check—for example, executing code or observing the result of an action. Then there’s a signal beyond another model’s judgment. But even with that, you need to test whether the improvement carries over to new situations. Producing a better answer after feedback and generalizing better behavior are two different accomplishments.

r001.rationale: It says correcting one prompt does not necessarily prevent the same mistake on differently phrased questions or questions requiring different reasoning, communicating that critique cannot guarantee generalization across prompts.

r002.rationale: It discusses limits of repeated critique and the value of independent checks, but does not identify greater prompt coverage as a benefit of making critique more scalable.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key distinction is between being able to critique an answer and being able to turn that critique into a general improvement. If you give a model feedback on one particular prompt, it may fix that answer, but that doesn’t necessarily mean it will behave better on a different prompt that requires the same underlying skill.

And the critique itself has limits. If the critic shares the same blind spots as the model generating the answer, you can get a process where the answer looks increasingly convincing without actually becoming more correct. So I think automated critique is especially useful when you have something you can verify independently, like executing code or checking a prediction against an environment.

The harder question is how you take those individual corrections and learn a principle that transfers. You need to evaluate that on new problems, because improving the answer you’re currently critiquing is a much weaker result than improving the model’s behavior more broadly.

r001.rationale: It says feedback on one prompt may not transfer to another and urges testing on new problems, but does not state that critique cannot guarantee coverage of every possible prompt.

r002.rationale: The response discusses scalability only indirectly through generalization and independent verification; it does not identify greater prompt coverage as a benefit of scaling automated critique.
